name: Beth Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate French into English for an agency that works with drug companies, so it's patient leaflets, consent forms for medical trials and the odd hospital discharge letter. Twice a week I'm also on call for phone interpreting with a hospital switchboard, usually a French-speaking patient in A&E (the emergency department). I work at a fold-out desk in our spare room with two screens and a big medical dictionary I bought second-hand. I like the precision; I don't like that the agency's reviewers find more mistakes in my work than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, Tom, who drives a city bus on shifts. We rent a two-bed flat on the edge of town, and between us we've got about three weeks of money saved after his car broke down in the summer. There's nowhere local that hires translators, so it's all online or by phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say medical translation still needs careful human checking, because a wrong dose on a leaflet hurts someone. At the agency's online meetings I'd say the AI helps with glossaries but not much else. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm already worried, AI or not. The agency gave me a warning about quality in the spring, and if they drop me, I'd lose most of my income. Tom's wage covers rent but not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools a bit more for terminology checks, since I make most of my mistakes there. I'd ask the agency's senior reviewer for feedback every month, so I improve faster. And we'd cut takeaways and put twenty-five a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On edge, a bit. Not because of AI, but because I'm not as good as I need to be yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the quality warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mistranslated a dosage unit on a leaflet draft, micrograms as milligrams, and the reviewer caught it. Nobody was hurt, because that's what reviewers are for. But I cried in the bathroom for twenty minutes, and I check every unit three times now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing the agency mean for you and Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd survive on Tom's wage, just about, if we stopped everything else. I'd probably take more hospital phone shifts and maybe call-centre work. It would feel like I'd let him down.

AI helps with **glossaries**, but not much else.
think: I'm already worried because of a **quality warning** from the agency.
My partner's **bus wage** covers rent but little more.
do: Use AI tools more for **terminology checks**.
Ask the senior reviewer for **monthly feedback**.
Cut takeaways and save **twenty-five a week**.
feel: **On edge** because her skill isn't yet where it needs to be.
S0.quote: I mistranslated a dosage unit on a leaflet draft, micrograms as milligrams, and the reviewer caught it.
fieldNote: Her worry stems from **her own skill**, not from AI.
A **quality warning** makes her income feel fragile even in a calm world.
Her **partner's wage** is a thin backstop.

steps.text: Use AI glossary tools to check medical terms on every leaflet
Ask the agency's senior reviewer for feedback every month
Stop takeaways and save twenty-five a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say patient leaflets will always need a human sign-off, because regulators require it. I'd also say translators will become reviewers. That's the sensible line, and I'd believe most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the reviewers keep their jobs, and the junior translators like me don't. The AI will produce the first draft, and the agency will want people who can catch errors, which is my weak spot. I'd expect my work to drop by half within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a short online course on medical post-editing, to show the agency I can check machine drafts. I'd also look into pharmacy technician training at the college, because I like the medical side and it's partly hands-on. We'd cut the gym memberships and Tom would pick up overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have something to do, which helps me. I'm better when I have a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pharmacy technician is a big change. What draws you to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already know the drug names and the units, painfully well now. And it's a job in a building, with a contract and a uniform, counting and checking things in your hands. My aunt is one, and she's never been out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Tom feel about doing more overtime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says it's fine, but he's tired. His shifts already start at five some days. I'd feel bad about it, so I'd want the course to be short.

**Pharmacy technician** work builds on what she already knows.
She is **uncomfortable** leaning on her partner's overtime.

steps.text: Take a short online course in medical post-editing
Apply for pharmacy technician training at the college
Rely on her partner's bus overtime for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and the government needs to step in quickly. I'd share practical advice online, like where to find retraining money. I wouldn't be one of the angry ones, just a worried one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my translation work is gone within two years, and even pharmacy technician work changes because the checking is thinking work. Tom's bus is safer for longer, until the robots and self-driving come around 2031. We'd be living on one wage for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the pharmacy technician course straight away and do care shifts at weekends, because hands-on work lasts three more years. We'd move somewhere cheaper, maybe a one-bed closer to Tom's depot. And we'd put off any talk of a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like the ground's tilting and I'm grabbing the nearest thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned putting off a wedding. Had you been planning one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loosely, for 2028. Tom proposed last Christmas with his grandmother's ring. We'd keep the ring and drop the party. You can't spend money on a wedding party when one of you has no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about money that first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Tom that I'll pay him back when I'm working again. He'd say we're a team, which is true and still makes me feel small.

say: It's **frightening**, and the government must step in quickly.
I'd share **practical advice** online about where to find retraining money.
think: My **translation work** is gone within two years.
We'd live on **one wage** until robots reach buses around 2031.
do: Start the **pharmacy technician** course straight away.
Do **weekend care shifts** for the three years before robots.
Move to a cheaper **one-bed** near her partner's depot.
S2.quote: You can't spend money on a wedding party when one of you has no job.
fieldNote: She uses the **robot gap** for weekend care work.
Her **wedding plans** are the first thing to go.
She feels **small** depending on her partner, despite his support.

steps.text: Start the pharmacy technician course at the college
Take weekend shifts at a local care home
Move to a cheaper one-bed flat near the bus depot
Postpone the 2028 wedding party and keep the ring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to plan sensibly, and I'd want the agency to be honest about its timetable. I'd tell friends to start retraining early. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose translation work around 2029, before AGI officially arrives. But I'd finish the pharmacy technician course by then, and the hands-on side of it lasts until about 2034. That's a real bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating while I study part-time for two years, using AI tools to work faster. I'd aim to save two months of money by 2029. Tom and I would still marry, small, in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd see a path. Less like falling, more like a steep walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the wedding stay in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have a plan and a course. With five years, you can still make normal choices, just carefully. Tom's mum would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finding the exact phrase a patient will understand at two in the morning on the phone. That's the bit I'm actually good at. Nobody tells you that the plain words are the hardest ones.

I'd want the agency to be **honest** about its timetable.
think: I'd lose translation work around **2029**, before AGI officially arrives.

do: Study **part-time** for two years while translating with AI tools.
feel: **Worried** but able to see a path, like a steep walk.
S3.quote: Nobody tells you that the plain words are the hardest ones.
fieldNote: Time turns pharmacy work into a **real bridge**.
The **wedding** stays in, which shows how time restores normal choices.
She is proudest of **plain-language** phone interpreting.

steps.text: Study pharmacy technician training part-time for two years
Use AI tools to finish leaflet jobs faster
Save two months of expenses by 2029
Hold a small wedding with her partner in 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make sensible plans, and I'd encourage people not to panic. I'd say translators should move into related fields early. I'd probably sound quite positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be squeezed out of translation in the next few years, just more slowly. But with a decade I could qualify as a pharmacist, not just a technician, which pays better. That changes things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and get better, with AI help, for the next three years, and save. Around 2029 I'd apply for a pharmacy degree with a student loan. We'd plan a child for after I qualify, maybe 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It's a long project, but I like long projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A pharmacy degree is also thinking work. Doesn't AGI reach that in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, but by then I'd be qualified and working in a hospital pharmacy, partly hands-on. I'm not sure it saves me. A pharmacy degree gives me ten years of decent work, which is more than translation offers now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money during the degree. A student loan and Tom's bus wage, with rent going up every year, is tight. If his route gets automated early, we'd be in trouble.

Translators should move into **related fields** early, before the work dries up.

steps.text: Translate leaflets with AI help for three more years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be halfway through retraining with no income and the wedding off. What would help is paid retraining for people in medical translation to move into health jobs, with a wage while we study. The hospitals are short of staff anyway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients on the phone. When someone is scared in A&E at two in the morning, the right word matters more than the fast word. I hope somebody is still checking those words.

headlineQuote: When someone is scared in A&E at two in the morning, the right word matters more than the fast word.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** French–English medical translator and on-call hospital phone interpreter.
She rents with her partner, a **bus driver**, and they have about three weeks of savings.
A recent **quality warning** makes her doubt her skill and her income even before AI.
Steady and practical, she plans a move into **pharmacy** work, aiming higher when there's more time.
Her mood runs **anxious to alarmed**, and her wedding and family plans move with the warning time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, halfway through retraining with no income and the wedding off.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** from medical translation into health jobs, with a wage while studying.
